extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy of science (and anyone evaluating or constructing inductive arguments)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for assessing inductive inferences, the role of syllogistic premises, axioms, hypotheses, and methods of proof in philosophical and scientific argumentation. Useful for reviewers judging the soundness and justification of generalizations from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major and minor assertions proved together by same evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Both admit that when we say, All men are mortal, we make an assertion reaching beyond the sphere of our knowledge of individual cases; ... when a new individual, Socrates, is brought within the field of our knowledge ... we learn that we have already made an assertion respecting Socrates without knowing it: our own general formula being, to that extent, for the first time interpreted to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill contends that the smaller (particular) assertion is not proved by the larger (general) alone; rather both are proved together by the same grounds of experience on which the general assertion was made. Evaluate arguments by checking whether both general and particular claims rest on the same experiential justification, not by treating the minor as deriving truth from the major alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office of the minor premise: show that the comparison has been made
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that this comparison has been made, is the office of the minor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The minor premise functions to indicate that the new individual possesses the marks (the precise kind of likeness) required by the general formula. When assessing reasoning, verify that the minor explicitly identifies the relevant likeness between the particular case and observed cases, rather than merely naming a class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogistic premises are precautions, not necessary conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: They are not the conditions of reasoning, but a precaution against erroneous reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that formal major/minor syllogisms are devices for clarification and error-prevention. Assess whether a purportedly 'syllogistic' argument actually adds evidence, or merely restates experiential grounds in formal language; do not require syllogistic form as the sole validity criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor as 'Socrates is like A, B, C' — universal type of the minor
rubrics_metrics.description: The only minor premise necessary to reasoning in the example under consideration, is, Socrates is like A, B, C, and the other individuals who are known to have died. And this is the only universal type of that step in the reasoning process which is represented by the minor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating particulars-to-particulars inferences, expect the minor to assert similarity to observed instances rather than to name a class. Check that the asserted similarity captures the relevant properties for the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expediency of determining beforehand the kind of likeness (the major)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience ... teaches the expediency of determining beforehand what kind of likeness to the cases observed, is necessary to bring an unobserved case within the same predicate; and the answer to this question is the major.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the generalization (major) specifies which resemblances are relevant for projecting predicates to unobserved cases. Good arguments make explicit which features are the justificatory marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by approximation (method of concomitant variations / limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who employ this argument ... show themselves unfamiliar with a common and perfectly valid mode of inductive proof; proof by approximation. ... The inference that if they had no breadth or flexure at all, they would inclose no space at all, is a correct inductive inference ... conformable to ... the Method of Concomitant Variations; of which the mathematical Doctrine of Limits presents the extreme case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate inductive claims that appeal to idealized limits by checking empirical gradations and concomitant variation. A legitimate inductive move can justify conclusions about ideal cases if supported by a converging series of approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses as partly fictional but useful assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypotheses spoken of in the text are of a different character; they are known not to be literally true, while as much of them as is true is not hypothetical, but certain. ... This unreal exactitude might be called a fiction, as properly as an hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging hypotheses, distinguish between the idealized (known not literally true) assumptions used for reasoning and the certain elements they contain. Accept hypotheses that serve as useful fictions so long as their true components are identified and justified relative to experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms and definitions often are generalizations from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The truths of geometry are summed up and embodied in its definitions and axioms.... Those which declare that two straight lines can not inclose a space, and that two straight lines which cut one another can not both be parallel to a third, are in reality the only ones which express characteristic properties of space ... carry their inductive origin on the face of their enunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess axioms by their empirical origin and continual suggestion by experience. Don't demand purely a priori derivation; evaluate whether axioms are justified as widely corroborated generalizations from observed regularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms of mechanics are inductive, not self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: As we admit no such propositions, other than as truths inductively collected from observation, even in geometry itself, it can hardly be expected that, in a science of obviously contingent relations, we should acquiesce in a contrary view. ... What but experience ... can possibly inform us that a force so applied will have any tendency to turn the lever on its centre at all?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In appraising mechanical or physical axioms, require appeal to accumulated observation and practical trials rather than pure intuition. Check for implicit idealizations (e.g., rigid lines) and whether empirical practice supports the axiom's generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental images and recollection as experimental resources when precise
rubrics_metrics.description: We may, and continually do, study nature in our recollections, when the objects themselves are absent; and in the case of geometrical forms we can perfectly, but in most other cases only imperfectly, trust our recollections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether reasoning that relies on vivid mental representations is warranted: for simple geometrical forms recollection can be a reliable basis; for complex sensory qualities (colors, odors) recollection is less precise and should be treated cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction in science vs. everyday inference: generality and record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: To the idea of Science, an express recognition and distinct apprehension of general laws as such, is essential: but nine-tenths of the conclusions drawn from experience in the course of practical life, are drawn without any such recognition: they are direct inferences from known cases, to a case supposed to be similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing scientific work, expect explicit general laws and recorded generalizations; when reviewing practical reasoning, accept direct inferences from particulars but check whether they are equivalent in structure to scientific inductions and whether they lack security that formal generalization provides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple explanations can be consistent if developed to match facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Undoubtedly all these explanations may be true and consistent with each other, and would be so if each had been followed out so as to show in what manner it could be made consistent with the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dogmatic exclusion of alternative models or explanations; evaluate whether competing theories can be reconciled by showing empirical equivalence or by making explicit which parts are literal claims versus representational devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of error arises mainly from initial assumptions and from ambiguity, not mere length of argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The point we are discussing is the fallibility not of the premises, but of the reasoning, as distinguished from the premises. Now the validity of the reasoning depends always upon the same axiom, repeated (in thought) 'over and over again' ... Mr. Spencer's second answer is valid up to a certain point; it is, that every prolongation of the process involves additional chances of casual error, from carelessness in the reasoning operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating long chains of reasoning, distinguish between inherent logical risk (rooted in initial untrustworthy assumptions) and accidental risks (carelessness, ambiguous terms). Focus peer review on clarifying ambiguous terminology and checking first-step assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about relying on inconceivability of the negation as proof
rubrics_metrics.description: My position is that this assertion can not be a necessary part of the argument. ... I derive none of its evidence from so very untrustworthy a test as the inconceivableness of the negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept arguments that rest chiefly on the claim that the negation is 'inconceivable.' Demand empirical or principled grounds for assertions rather than appeals to mere inconceivability.
